title: Sharjah Wants $3 Billion From Indian Investors as Hormuz Chaos Reshapes Trade
excerpt: Invest in Sharjah CEO Mohamed Juma Al Musharrkh says the emirate is targeting $3 billion in Indian investment by 2027, with a $2 billion Khorfakkan port upgrade and Hormuz disruptions pulling cargo to the UAE's east coast.
body:
• Sharjah is targeting $3 billion from Indian investors by 2027, with Invest in Sharjah CEO Mohamed Juma Al Musharrkh expecting Indian investment to grow 15% year-on-year, according to The Economic Times.
  • The pitch is anchored by a $2 billion upgrade of Khorfakkan port on the UAE's east coast — outside the Strait of Hormuz, which has been effectively shut since the US-Iran conflict began in March 2026, pushing cargo to alternative routes.
  • Sharjah already accounts for around 40% of the UAE's industrial establishments and roughly a third of its manufacturing output, with more than 2,800 factories across 21 industrial zones and investors from 113 nationalities.
  • What this means for you: Indian businesses can enter through Sharjah's 21 industrial zones and free zones, which offer full foreign ownership, zero currency restrictions and re-export access to Europe, Africa and the Middle East under the India-UAE CEPA framework. Indian business councils in the UAE run regular B2B matchmaking — the next major window is the Sharjah Investment Forum in October 2026.

Sharjah is making its most aggressive pitch yet for Indian capital, targeting $3 billion from Indian investors by 2027 as shipping disruptions around the Strait of Hormuz push businesses to rethink Gulf supply routes. Invest in Sharjah CEO Mohamed Juma Al Musharrkh expects Indian investment in the emirate to grow 15% year-on-year, according to The Economic Times.

"Sharjah has always had extremely close ties with India on both a business and community level, which has been reinforced by the extremely high calibre of authorities, government figures and private investors that were met."

— Mohamed Juma Al Musharrkh, CEO, Invest in Sharjah

The centerpiece of the pitch is geography. Sharjah's Khorfakkan port sits on the UAE's east coast, on the Gulf of Oman — outside the Strait of Hormuz, which has been effectively closed to most shipping since the US-Iran conflict began in March. A $2 billion upgrade of Khorfakkan is underway to absorb the diverted traffic, and the port operator Gulftainer plans to expand its capacity from 3.5 million TEU to 5 million TEU, with a longer-term target above 10 million TEU.

Context & Background

The Hormuz disruption is the most severe in decades. The strait carries roughly a fifth of global oil shipments each day; with it largely shut, Brent crude surged past $100 a barrel, container traffic collapsed, and businesses shifted to smaller ports, road transport, rail and air freight. Shipping costs between China and the UAE have risen along with insurance premiums, and Indian oil refiners — from Indian Oil to Reliance and Bharat Petroleum — have rewritten procurement terms to take shipping into their own hands.

https://x.com/EconomicTimes/status/2108034189459153349

The UAE has moved faster than most of the region to build workarounds. Its Abu Dhabi Crude Oil Pipeline already connects oil fields to Fujairah on the Gulf of Oman, and the country plans to double that capacity to 3.6 million barrels a day, potentially by mid-2027. Ports have been the sharper story: AD Ports has deployed hundreds of additional trucks, expanded rail services and opened sea connections with Oman, India, Pakistan and Red Sea ports. Gulftainer is also planning a new inland logistics hub at Al Dhaid, about 50 km from Khorfakkan — a dry port of more than 100 hectares costing over $100 million in its first phase alone.

Sharjah's pitch is not starting from zero. In an interview with Gulf Business ahead of this month's Sharjah Investment Forum — themed "Building Adaptive Economies" — Al Musharrkh noted that food and beverage made up 28% of the emirate's FDI projects in 2025, with consumer products another 20%, spread deliberately across industrial equipment, logistics, technology and manufacturing. FDI hit $1.5 billion in the first half of 2025 alone, up 361% year-on-year, with 74 new projects and 2,578 new jobs.

Impact & Analysis

The $3 billion target is ambitious but not implausible. Indian companies are already part of Sharjah's industrial story: recent projects include a warehouse and distribution hub by logistics firm Gxpress and a gold jewellery facility by Vinsmera Jewels. A recent Invest in Sharjah trade delegation to India — spanning health, education and media production — also discussed a Bollywood film production facility in the emirate, building on years of cultural ties.

Whether the Hormuz disruption becomes a durable advantage depends on two unknowns: how long the strait stays disrupted, and whether infrastructure built for the emergency retains its value when normal routes reopen. Sharjah's bet is that diversification — 113 investor nationalities, up from 97 a year earlier — insulates it either way.

Diaspora Angle

The UAE hosts 3.3 million expatriate Indians, the largest non-resident Indian community in the world, and Sharjah's industrial base already runs on Indian talent and capital. For NRI entrepreneurs, the current moment combines a weaker alternative — Gulf ports inside Hormuz are constrained — with active dealmaking: Shurooq, the Sharjah Investment and Development Authority, has been running matchmaking sessions with Indian business councils and captains of industry specifically to convert interest into projects.

What's Next

The Sharjah Investment Forum this month will be the next test of the $3 billion target, with FDI, AI and diversification on the agenda. For Indian investors weighing the move, the variables to watch are concrete: Khorfakkan's capacity expansion timeline, the Al Dhaid dry-port buildout, and any stabilization in Hormuz shipping — which would ease pressure on alternatives but would not undo the infrastructure already committed.
